Weaker Brother
WAY-ker BRUHTH-er
noun
From Romans 14 and 1 Corinthians 8; the believer weak in faith or conscience, whom the stronger must not wound but bear.

📖 Biblical Definition

The weaker brother is the believer who, weak in faith or tender in conscience, scruples over matters that Scripture has left indifferent—meats, days, and the like—and whom the stronger brother is charged to receive, bear with, and not to wound. Paul treats him in Romans and First Corinthians: Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations; for one believeth that he may eat all things: another, who is weak, eateth herbs. The matters in view are things truly indifferent—not sins, not the plain commands of God, but disputable practices on which a tender conscience may err in scruple. The stronger brother, who rightly understands his liberty, is not to despise the weak, nor the weak to judge the strong; rather the strong is to forbear the use of his liberty where it would wound the weak brother’s conscience or embolden him to sin against it: it is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth. Love limits liberty: when ye sin so against the brethren, and wound their weak conscience, ye sin against Christ. Yet this forbearance concerns indifferent things only; it is no license to surrender the truth of the gospel or the commands of God to another’s scruple. The dictionary honors the doctrine of the weaker brother as a charge of love—that the strong bear the infirmities of the weak, and limit their liberty for the brother’s good—against both the selfish use of liberty that wounds, and the legalism that would bind all consciences to one man’s scruple.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The believer weak in faith or conscience over indifferent things, whom the stronger must receive and not wound; love limits liberty for the brother’s good.

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 14:1 — "Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations."

Rom 14:21 — "It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak."

1Co 8:12 — "But when ye sin so against the brethren, and wound their weak conscience, ye sin against Christ."

1Co 8:9 — "But take heed lest by any means this liberty of yours become a stumblingblock to them that are weak."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The weaker-brother principle is stretched to bind all consciences to one scruple, or ignored by a selfish use of liberty; Scripture charges love that limits liberty in things indifferent.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond two opposite abuses. The first stretches the weaker-brother principle into a tyranny of the scrupulous, by which the most easily offended conscience binds the whole church, forbidding every liberty lest someone stumble—turning Paul’s charge of love into a new legalism. But Paul’s concern is for the genuine weak brother in danger of being wounded or emboldened to sin against conscience, not for the perpetually offended who would rule others by their scruples. The second abuse is the selfish use of liberty that despises the weak and wounds them without care.

The principle to recover is love that limits liberty in things indifferent, for the brother’s good. The matters in view are truly indifferent—meats, days, disputable practices—not sins, nor the plain commands of God, nor the truths of the gospel. In these, the strong is to receive the weak, not to doubtful disputations (Rom 14:1), and to forbear his liberty where it would cause a brother to stumble: it is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth (Rom 14:21). To wound a weak brother’s conscience is to sin against Christ (1 Cor 8:12); liberty must not become a stumblingblock (1 Cor 8:9). Yet this forbearance is bounded: it concerns indifferent things, and is no license to surrender the truth of the gospel or the commands of God. Love limits liberty for the weak, but love also holds the truth fast.
